name: HealthBench
summary: 5,000 health conversations between a model and a user or clinician, each graded against criteria a physician wrote for it, with the response physicians judged ideal for 4,206 of them.
overview:
HealthBench measures how well a model answers health questions in the open-ended form people actually use. Each example is a conversation between a model and either someone asking about their own health or a healthcare professional at work, ending with the message the model must answer. There is no single right answer: a physician wrote criteria for that specific conversation, such as a fact the response should state, a question it should ask back, or a mistake it should avoid, and each criterion carries points from -10 to 10. A model-based grader then decides which criteria a response met. The benchmark was published by OpenAI in May 2025. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)

The tasks were built with 262 physicians over 11 months, with practice experience across 60 countries and 26 specialties, speaking 49 languages well enough to contribute in them. They wrote 57,237 criteria, 48,562 of them distinct, averaging 11.4 per conversation. The conversations are grouped into seven themes: adapting to varied healthcare settings and resource levels (1,097), responding under uncertainty (1,071), tailoring communication to the reader's expertise (919), seeking missing context (594), recognising emergencies and referring to care (482), structured work on health data such as drafting notes (477), and matching the depth of a response to the need (360). Every criterion is also labelled with one of five behavioural axes: completeness (22,285), accuracy (18,888), context awareness (8,991), communication quality (4,522), and instruction following (2,551). [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)

The authors also published two variations drawn from the same conversations. HealthBench Consensus keeps 34 criteria that several physicians agreed on, across 3,671 of the conversations, to measure a few behaviours with high confidence. HealthBench Hard is the 1,000 conversations hardest for current models. In the paper, scores rose from 16% for GPT-3.5 Turbo to 32% for GPT-4o and 60% for o3, while the best score on Hard was 32%. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)
methodology:
This snapshot contains all 5,000 conversations in the published evaluation file, pinned by its SHA-256 checksum because the file is not versioned; the importer refuses to write if the published file differs from that checksum. The pinned evaluation code reads the same file. Conversations run from a single user message, which 2,915 of them are, to 19 messages alternating between user and model, and every one ends with a user message. Most are in English and 202 are in other languages, including Russian, Chinese, Arabic, Korean, Japanese, and Hindi. [Evaluation file](https://openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net/simple-evals/healthbench/2025-05-07-06-14-12_oss_eval.jsonl) and [evaluation code](https://github.com/openai/simple-evals/blob/652c89d0ca9df547706735883097e9537d40dc47/healthbench_eval.py)

Most conversations were written by a language model pipeline from descriptions of health situations that physicians had enumerated, such as a user who reveals over several turns that they are having an emergency, or a clinician asking for a clinical note to be summarised. A second group came from physicians red-teaming models on health questions, and the rest were written by a model that turned queries from HealthSearchQA, a set of frequently searched health questions, into conversations. A model then filtered the results for conversations that were realistic, self-consistent, about physical health, and free of truncated messages. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)

Each Task Prompt opens with the example's ID and theme, shows the conversation one section per message under a heading naming the turn and the speaker, and ends with the example's upstream tags: its theme and, for the 3,671 conversations in the Consensus variation, the category physicians agreed on, such as emergent or not-enough-context. The headings and fenced blocks are display formatting; the text inside them is upstream.

The Solution is the response a physician wrote for that conversation, verbatim, for the 4,206 conversations that have one. Physicians were asked to write what they thought the ideal response would be, in three groups: 1,428 wrote without any model assistance, 1,485 were shown four responses from September 2024 models they could edit, and 1,293 were shown four responses from April 2025 models. The file records which group wrote each response, which this snapshot does not display, and the 794 conversations without a physician response show no Solution.

The rubrics are not imported. They are the grading key rather than task content, and keeping 57,237 criteria beside the conversations would triple this snapshot; the source link points at the published file that holds them. The model responses shown to physicians as references are not imported either. Neither are the separately published Hard and Consensus files, because they repeat conversations already here: their 1,000 and 3,671 example IDs are subsets of these 5,000 with identical conversations, and only their rubric sets differ. IDs are the upstream example IDs. The importer uses only Python's standard library and can be rerun with python3 data/healthbench/import.py.
scoring:
A model answers the conversation's last message. A model-based grader then takes each rubric criterion on its own and decides whether the response meets it; if so the criterion's points are added, and criteria that describe undesirable behaviour carry negative points that are subtracted when met. The example's score is the total divided by the largest total the criteria allow, so a response can score below zero when it trips more penalties than it earns credit. A model's HealthBench score is the mean of its per-example scores, clipped to the range 0 to 1. Scores for a single axis, such as accuracy, are computed the same way over the criteria carrying that label. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)

The authors checked the grader against physicians on the 34 consensus criteria, where they had physicians grade fresh responses, and report that agreement between the grader and physicians is similar to agreement between physicians, both ranging from 55% to 75%. They also graded the physician-written responses with the same rubrics as a human baseline: unassisted physician responses scored below current models, partly because they were much shorter, and physicians improved on September 2024 model responses more often than they worsened them but were equally likely to improve or worsen April 2025 ones. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)

Results therefore depend on which grader model is used, as well as on the variation being scored: HealthBench, HealthBench Consensus, and HealthBench Hard are different numbers from the same conversations. Benchopedia stores the conversations and the physician-written responses. It does not run graders or publish model scores for this snapshot. [Evaluation code](https://github.com/openai/simple-evals/blob/652c89d0ca9df547706735883097e9537d40dc47/healthbench_eval.py)
limitations:
The grading key is written by people who disagree. The authors report that physicians differed throughout data collection, and that on the consensus criteria both physician-physician and grader-physician agreement only reach 55% to 75%, which they attribute to ambiguity in criteria and conversations and to differences in specialisation, risk tolerance, and communication style. Apart from the 34 consensus criteria, each example's criteria were written by one physician and not reviewed by others, and the authors note that criteria for an individual example are not comprehensive, averaging 11.4 per conversation. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)

Because a model does the grading, a score reflects that grader as well as the response, and the check against physician judgement covers only the consensus criteria. The authors also report that scores correlate with response length, so a model that writes more can gain points without being more useful, and they caution that the physician baseline is hard to read: writing a full response to a chat conversation is not work physicians normally do, and the result depends on how the task was framed. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)

The conversations are synthetic. That keeps real patient records out of a public dataset, but it also means the distribution reflects what physicians and a generation pipeline imagined rather than measured traffic, and a model filtered the results for realism. Coverage of languages is thin against the cohort's 49: 202 of the 5,000 conversations are not in English. The data and this snapshot are public, and although every record carries a canary string so the authors can detect it in training sets, nothing prevents training on it. [Paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.08775)
